titre: Akhenaten, Aten, and the Myth of the First Monotheist
accroche: Around 1350 BCE, a pharaoh closes Egypt's temples and leaves only one god standing: the sun disk.
contenu_vulgarise:
Around 1353 BCE, the pharaoh Akhenaten founded a new city, Akhetaten, far from Thebes and its temples. There he imposed the exclusive worship of Aten, the sun disk, and had the sanctuaries of Egypt's other gods closed, Amun first among them.

## A Hymn to a God Without Equal

The fullest trace of this religion is a text carved in the tomb of the courtier Ay, at Amarna: the Great Hymn to the Aten. It describes a single god, creator of the world, who assigns each person his place, distinguishes the languages and skin colors of men, and whose rising and setting govern the life and death of all things: animals, plants, humans. Specialists see in it one of the most accomplished pieces of Egyptian religious poetry, predating by several centuries the biblical Psalms to which it is often compared: as early as 1912, Breasted found in it a sensitivity to the presence of God in nature that he judged comparable to that of the Hebrew psalms, written, in his view, a thousand years later. Other scholars see only a resemblance of genre between two neighboring religious traditions, with no demonstrated borrowing from one to the other.

Akhenaten does not merely disown the other gods: he erases their images and, in some cases, removes their names from inscriptions. But his reign lasts only about seventeen years. At his death, his successors reopen the temples, return to the worship of Amun, and in their turn hammer Akhenaten's name off the monuments he left behind.

## What This Shifts

In 1939, in *Moses and Monotheism*, Sigmund Freud took up this story and turned it around: Moses, he claimed, had been an Egyptian priest who remained faithful to the religion of Aten after Akhenaten's death, and carried this monotheistic faith to the Hebrew people. The hypothesis is seductive: it would give monotheism a dated beginning, a named founder, a demonstrable continuity. It is supported by no document: no Egyptian or biblical source links Moses to Akhenaten's court, and Freud himself acknowledges this by presenting his book as a construction, not a demonstration.

The tenacious myth is therefore not only that of a heretic pharaoh: it is, more recently, that of a single, traceable origin of monotheism, in which ancient Egypt would pass directly to the Bible an idea it had invented on its own. Atenism vanished within a generation, with no avowed successor; what gives it, three thousand years later, the role of first monotheism owes as much to the psychoanalytic imagination of the 20th century as to the hieroglyphs found at Amarna.

repere.texte: The Great Hymn to the Aten, carved in the tomb of the courtier Ay at Amarna, dates from the reign of Akhenaten, around 1353-1336 BCE.
repere.source: Wikipedia (contributors), Great Hymn to the Aten

carte.punch: The idea that Akhenaten invented monotheism comes as much from Freud as from ancient Egypt.
carte.idee: Around 1353 BCE, Akhenaten imposes the exclusive worship of the sun disk Aten. In 1939, Freud makes it, in Moses and Monotheism, the hidden origin of the Hebrew religion: a psychoanalytic hypothesis that no document supports.

quiz.question: Why is Freud's theory linking Akhenaten to Moses not an established historical fact?
choix: Because Akhenaten's very existence as a pharaoh is not confirmed by archaeology
Because the worship of Aten never mentioned a single or creator god
Because Freud retracted this theory before his book was published in 1939
Because it rests on a psychoanalytic reconstruction, with no documentary trace of a transmission between the two
quiz.explication: No document attests to a link between Akhenaten and Moses: Freud builds a psychoanalytic hypothesis, published without retraction in 1939. Akhenaten, by contrast, is well attested archaeologically, and the Great Hymn to the Aten explicitly describes a single, creator god.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What happens to the worship of Aten after Akhenaten's death?
choix: It becomes the official religion of Egypt for the following centuries
It is abandoned by his successors, who reopen the temples of the other gods
It spreads throughout the ancient Near East
It merges with the worship of Amun to form a new religion
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Akhenaten's successors quickly return to the worship of Amun and the other gods, and even hammer his name off the monuments: the worship of Aten becomes neither a lasting official religion, nor a regional one, nor a merger with Amun.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What does the Great Hymn to the Aten, carved in the tomb of the courtier Ay, describe?
choix: A single, creator god, whose rising and setting govern life and death
A military victory of Akhenaten over the priests of Amun
The account of the construction of the city of Akhetaten
The list of pharaohs who preceded Akhenaten on the throne
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The Great Hymn describes a single, creator god who assigns each person's place and whose rising and setting govern the life and death of all things; it recounts neither a battle, nor the building of a city, nor a dynastic list.
